prompt.context: You're the new CEO of a home appliance company. The industry has four major players and has experienced sluggish growth over the past decade. You have risen through the ranks, starting in corporate strategy after graduating from CBS. The firm has a long history as providers of durable, middle-market, home goods. The industry has been stable for years, equally split between 4 large, multinational competitors. On your way to your first meeting with the Board, you are stuck in traffic with your R&D Vice President. He mentions to you that he has developed a new product for the washer & dryer division — the first major innovation in the industry in years. The product is a combined washer and dryer in one unit (i.e. you put clothes in and set it to both wash and dry). You predict the board will ask you what you want to do with this potential new product, and you have 15 minutes in traffic to figure out what to do.
prompt.question: What should you do with this new combined washer/dryer product?

clarifying_info.q: What is the price and cost of the new combo unit?
clarifying_info.a: Price to consumer: $700 per unit. Manufacturing cost: $550 per unit. Total profit: $150 per unit.

clarifying_info.q: What is the price and cost of the current separate washer and dryer?
clarifying_info.a: Price to consumer: $500 each ($1,000 total). Manufacturing cost: $400 per unit. Total profit: $200 per pair.

clarifying_info.q: Are there competing products or is anyone else developing a similar product?
clarifying_info.a: No one else has begun R&D on this product. We would be the only ones with this product for 3 years.

clarifying_info.q: Are retailers or distribution channels an issue?
clarifying_info.a: Collaborators such as floor space, retailer cannibalization, and current sales cannibalization are not a substantial issue.

clarifying_info.q: Should we consider industrial or business customers?
clarifying_info.a: Do not consider businesses or industrial use. Only look at households.

framework: Financial Assessment: market size and growth; revenue and cost to derive profit for both current and new product; current vs. potential sales mix; R&D spend to date and remaining investment needed; NPV of the project; breakeven timeline
Firm Analysis: cannibalization of existing sales; patentability; changes in skill set, culture, and divisions; retailer skill sets
Customer: who is the current customer vs. the new target customer; single unit saves space — primarily an urban customer
Competition: expected competitive response; how long before a competitor copies the product
Channels: current distribution (big box, Walmart, mom-and-pop) and whether that changes with the new product

questions.prompt: What is the market size for the combined washer/dryer product?
questions.guidance: Candidate should build a structured market sizing from US population down to annual washer/dryer purchases, focusing on households only (no industrial/business use).

math.setup: Start with US population, divide by average household size, apply penetration and purchase-frequency rates.
steps: 80% of households have a washer and dryer = 80M households
80% live in urban or suburban areas = 64M households
Households buy a washer/dryer every 10 years → 64M / 10 = 6.4M units purchased per year
math.answer: Approximately 6.4 million combined washer/dryer units could be purchased per year.

questions.prompt: Evaluate the economics of the combined washer/dryer product. Is it more or less profitable than the existing separate units?
questions.guidance: Candidate should compare per-unit profit of the combo ($150) vs. the traditional pair ($200), recognize the $50 per-unit profit loss, and then perform a breakeven analysis to determine what incremental market share is needed to offset the profit loss.

math.setup: The combo unit earns $50 less per sale than a traditional pair. Use current 25% market share as the baseline to quantify the total annual profit loss, then compute how many additional units — and what incremental market share — must be captured to break even.
steps: Annual profit loss = $50/unit × 6.4M units × 25% current market share = $80M
Additional units needed to break even = $80M ÷ $150 profit per unit = ~0.53M units
Incremental market share needed = 0.53M ÷ 6.4M = ~8.3%, or roughly 12% of total market (varies by rounding approach in casebook)
Current share is 25%; gaining ~12 percentage points represents ~50% growth in market share
math.answer: The combo unit is less profitable per unit ($150 vs $200). To break even on the profit loss, the company needs to capture roughly 12 additional percentage points of market share — about a 50% increase over the current 25% share.

questions.prompt: Based on your analysis, what do you recommend the company do with the new combined product?
questions.guidance: Candidate should commit to a clear recommendation (launch or do not launch) and defend it with a strategic rationale. Two defensible positions exist. A strong candidate proactively acknowledges the counterarguments and explains why their conclusion still holds.

questions.prompt: The R&D VP now tells you that $20 million has already been sunk into the project, and it is unclear how much more will be needed to bring it to market. Also, the company has seen many CEOs come and go recently. This is one of your first major decisions. Does that change your answer?
questions.guidance: The interviewer is deliberately creating doubt to test whether the candidate can defend their recommendation under pressure. The sunk cost ($20M) should be treated as irrelevant to the forward-looking decision. The candidate should also address the CEO tenure signal — one strong response is to commit to being CEO for the long haul and use this product decision to signal a new era of innovation. The candidate should not simply flip their recommendation; they should engage with the new information and explain whether and why it changes the calculus.

recommendation: OPPOSE: Recommend stopping development. The new product has a lower per-unit profit margin ($150 vs $200) and would require capturing roughly 50% more market share just to break even on the profit loss — an ambitious target in a stable, mature market.

SUPPORT: Recommend continuing development. The combo unit is a flagship innovation that signals a new era of growth. First-mover advantage of 3 years, a clear target customer (urban households where space is constrained), and the potential to grow total market share in a stagnant industry justify the lower per-unit margin.
risks: A competitor may launch a similar product at lower cost or with superior distribution once the 3-year exclusivity window closes.
Consumer adoption may be slow if buyers are deeply entrenched in the idea of separate washer and dryer units.
next_steps: Explore whether the product can be targeted at industrial or commercial customers to avoid cannibalization of residential sales.
Meet with the marketing group to discuss how to position and price the product for urban customers.
